listening.title: Evaluating the Campus Peer-Support Programme
listening.script: Maya: So for our psychology methods presentation, we need to summarise the evaluation of the campus peer-support programme. Do you remember why it was set up? Josh: Yes, the counselling service was overloaded last year, so the university trained second-year volunteers to offer weekly listening sessions for first-year students feeling isolated. Maya: Right, mainly loneliness and study stress, not clinical treatment. I looked at the mid-year report. They ran an online survey and two focus groups. Josh: How many students actually responded to the survey? I wrote down two hundred. Maya: Actually, wait — the report first says two hundred were invited, but only one hundred and eighty completed it. So the response rate was still high, about ninety percent. Josh: Got it, one-eighty completed. What did they find? Maya: Overall satisfaction was quite positive. Around three-quarters said they felt more connected after four sessions. But the academic impact was less clear. Josh: You mean grades didn't really improve? Maya: Exactly. The report says there was no significant difference in average coursework marks between users and non-users. The authors suggest four sessions may be too short to affect performance. Josh: That makes sense. Did the focus groups explain why some students stopped coming? Maya: Yes. Several mentioned timetable clashes with part-time jobs, and a few said they wanted more practical study advice rather than just listening. One student said she expected tutoring, which was never the aim. Josh: So there's a mismatch in expectations. What limitation should we highlight? Maya: The biggest one is selection bias. Students chose to join, so they may have been more motivated than average. The report admits it cannot prove the programme caused the improvement in wellbeing. Josh: And it only covered one term, from October to December, so we don't know if benefits last. Maya: Perfect. Let's conclude that the evidence supports social benefits, but claims about academic results should remain cautious until a longer controlled study is done.

questions.title: Q1
questions.prompt: Why was the peer-support programme originally introduced?
options: To reduce pressure on counselling services
To train counsellors for clinical work
questions.explanation: The script links the programme to an overloaded counselling service, not replacement or grades. The clinical-work option misreads volunteer listening sessions.

questions.title: Q2
questions.prompt: What is corrected about the survey figures?
questions.explanation: Maya corrects the 200 figure to 180 completions from 200 invitations. The 90 figure confuses the ninety percent rate with a count.

questions.title: Q3
questions.prompt: What was the main academic finding?
options: Users gained significantly higher coursework marks
No clear difference in coursework marks
questions.explanation: The report found no significant mark difference, possibly due to short duration. The higher-marks option overstates the qualified claim.

questions.title: Q4
questions.prompt: Why did some students stop attending sessions?
questions.explanation: Timetable clashes with part-time jobs are stated directly. The listening-skills option is unsupported; the issue was expecting tutoring.

questions.title: Q5
questions.prompt: What limitation of the evaluation is emphasised?
options: The term studied was unusually quiet
questions.explanation: Self-selection means motivated joiners may bias wellbeing gains and block causal claims. The volunteers-only option misidentifies who was surveyed.

reading.title: How Reliable Are Low-Cost Air-Quality Monitors?
reading.passage: Cities increasingly rely on low-cost air-quality sensors to supplement official monitoring stations. Costing under three hundred dollars, these portable devices promise street-level data on fine particles known as PM2.5. A recent university study compared three popular models, labelled A, B and C, against a reference-grade analyser over twelve weeks in autumn. All three were placed on the same rooftop to ensure identical exposure to traffic and weather. In dry, stable conditions, Models A and B tracked the reference instrument closely, with average errors below fifteen percent. Model C consistently overestimated pollution, particularly in the morning, suggesting a calibration problem rather than random variation. The pattern changed markedly during humid weeks. When relative humidity exceeded eighty percent, all low-cost sensors reported higher values than the reference analyser. The researchers attribute this to water droplets being mistaken for particles by the optical counting method. Model A included a simple humidity correction in its software, which reduced but did not eliminate the bias. Model B had no correction, so its readings doubled on two foggy nights, even though reference levels remained moderate. These results illustrate a broader trade-off. Low-cost monitors provide far denser spatial coverage than the sparse official network, revealing differences between busy roads and parks that a single station would miss. However, their accuracy depends strongly on environmental conditions and maintenance. Dust accumulation on the sensor inlet, for example, gradually lowered readings in week ten until the devices were cleaned. The authors therefore argue that low-cost sensors are best viewed as complementary tools, not replacements for reference stations. They recommend regular co-location checks, where portable units are placed beside an official station to adjust their output, and transparent reporting of humidity and cleaning dates. As an example, the study describes a community group that mapped pollution near a school using Model A. The group correctly identified higher exposure during drop-off hours, but its absolute numbers were about twenty percent too high on damp days. The authors stress that this does not invalidate community monitoring; it means results should be interpreted as indicating patterns rather than precise legal exceedances. In conclusion, with careful calibration and qualified interpretation, low-cost monitors can extend public understanding, provided users acknowledge their limits.

questions.title: Q1
questions.prompt: What was the design of the university comparison?
options: Three models beside a reference analyser
One sensor tested in three cities
Three reference stations on one roof
Twelve models tested for one week
questions.explanation: The passage states three models shared a rooftop with a reference instrument for twelve weeks. The three-stations option reverses test and reference roles.

questions.title: Q2
questions.prompt: How did Models A and B perform when dry?
options: Only Model C gave stable readings
questions.explanation: Average errors below fifteen percent are reported for A and B in stable air. The foggy-night doubling applies only to Model B in humidity.

questions.title: Q3
questions.prompt: What can be inferred about Model B on foggy nights?
options: Its high readings reflected real pollution spikes
Its readings were inflated by moisture
Its inlet was blocked by dust
questions.explanation: Reference levels stayed moderate while B doubled, implying moisture misreading. The real-spike option ignores that reference comparison.

questions.title: Q4
questions.prompt: What is the authors' main claim illustrated by the school example?
options: Community data show patterns not precise levels
School drop-off causes no real pollution
Model A is accurate in all weather
questions.explanation: The example shows correct pattern detection but 20% overestimation on damp days. The replacement option contradicts the complementary-tools argument.

questions.title: Q5
questions.prompt: What do the authors recommend for reliable use?
options: Regular calibration checks and open reporting
questions.explanation: Co-location checks and reporting humidity and cleaning are explicitly recommended. The autumn-only option mistakes the study period for a usage rule.
